newsitem.title: USA: Germans make inroads into U.S. car market in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Germans make inroads into U.S. car market in 1996.

text.p: German carmakers posted stellar 1996 sales in the American market despite difficult conditions, but the glow may not last that long as industry executives view the New Year with cautious optimism.
The three major German carmakers -- BMW, Mercedes and Volkswagen -- all posted sharply higher sales last year in the United States.
With the North American International Auto Show underway in Detroit, many are reporting their best results in recent years.

BMW, for example, said it sold more than 100,000 vehicles in the United States for the first time in its history. Rival luxury carmaker Mercedes said it hoped to top that level in 1997 after selling about 95,000 vehicles in 1996.
Volkswagen, Europe's largest carmaker, reported its best results since 1990 while its luxury car unit, Audi, said sales rose more than 50 percent in 1996 to more than 27,000 vehicles.

But 1997 could prove to be more difficult for the carmakers, particularly since they still lag behind the Japanese in the U.S. import market amid new worries about Japan developing a counter-attack to the Germans' success.
Another problem is expectations of stagnant or little growth in the U.S. luxury vehicle market in the near term.
Yet turbulent foreign exchange markets, long a burden due to the strong mark, are finally starting to help German car exporters improve their profit outlook.
The head of the Audi business in America, Gerd Klauss, said in Detroit the Japanese would not be able to afford the losses they might incur in the U.S. market due to currency troubles.

That might prompt some German carmakers to consider a price war, he said. "The Japanese reinvest their profits back into the market," Klauss said. "No one, including the Europeans, can afford to hoard their money."

Fortunes have changed for German carmakers in the last few years, with many smarting from ridicule in the late 1980s for products with poor quality and service, limited options and excessively high prices.
"All of the German carmakers at the end of the 1980s were offering cars with too high prices due to cost structures at the time," Mercedes executive Juergen Hubbert told Reuters.

The reputation of quality German engineering was also dented when Audi saw most of its U.S. business come to a standstill over allegations that its cars were unsafe due to sudden acceleration problems.
Audi was cleared a few years later by the U.S. government but its handling of the situation -- essentially to blame the drivers for the problem -- was a public relations debacle.

During those critical years in the early 1990s when German cars were not in vogue in the United States -- particularly BMW and its image tied to the "Yuppie" 1980s -- the Japanese soaked up market share with a vengeance.

But German carmakers are seeing the fruits of their comeback, particularly Audi with its popular A4 sedan, BMW with its 3- and 5- series and Mercedes with its new SLK roadster, which has been tipped as a top car of the year.
The models are more tailored to the U.S. market and younger buyers, offering cars with more style and panache as well as better qualilty, according to industry observers.

German carmakers are also following the example of Japan in building new factories, such as BMW's plant in South Carolina and Mercedes's in Alabama, in a bid to build a "sympathy factor" to attract U.S. buyers.
